content.fullText: [00:00] We start with an adapted version of Leibniz's famous question, 'Why is there something rather than nothing?' Here we want to briefly understand why are there markets rather than no markets? Markets are a natural consequence of the way human beings behave. To unpack this statement, we need praxeology, which is the study of human action grounded on the Austrian school of economics. [00:27] Praxeology is the combination of two words: praxis and logic. In other words, the logic of practice or the logic of action. Some of the principles of praxeology can be traced back to the Greek philosophers, but the discipline was incorporated in the economic sciences by Carl Menger, the founder of the Austrian School of Economics, and Ludwig von Mises, one of the greatest economists of all time, and probably the most important of the 20th century. [00:58] Praxeology rests on a very basic and fundamental axiom called the Action Axiom. The Action Axiom states that human beings purposefully utilize means to achieve an end. This sounds obvious, but the subtle idea here is the idea of purpose. We only use means to achieve an end because we are motivated by a purpose, and that purpose is to create a better state of affairs in our lives. As we achieve this better state, the motivation remains intact, and we begin to move to the next slightly better state of affairs. This is the core of human action, and it's the basis for everything else that comes later. [01:36] Since we have this purpose to move towards a better state of affairs, that implies we must act, because nature has entropy, which is the tendency of things to go out of order if they are not properly maintained. Which means that if you don't act, you will move to a worse state of affairs very quickly. Just think about what happens if you do absolutely nothing for a long time. If you don't maintain at least your bodily functions, you will begin to perish. And to maintain things working, you need action and resources. [02:07] To act, we must have a mechanism that enables us to choose what the best action is. Given the almost infinite set of possible actions in every situation, we must choose one in detriment of all the others. That means we exchange all the possible actions we could have for the one we think is the most appropriate given our purpose to move towards a better state of affairs. [02:31] This means that EVERY decision you make is a TRADE! You are trading all the possible decisions you could make for the one you think is the best one to take. In other words, the idea of trading is a natural reflection of human nature, and it's much more primal and fundamental than what people usually realize because the general interpretation of trade is that it is a modern invention and a feature of capitalism. [02:56] In summary, the consequence of the Action Axiom is trading. If we don't act in the world, we die off. To act, we need to trade the set of all possible actions for the action we believe is the most appropriate. Trading is at the very basis of human nature. We do that with nature and with other human beings as well. Every single decision we make throughout our day is a trade. So, let's take a simple example that everybody deals with on a daily basis, which is the decision to wake up early or late. [03:28] You need a motivation to wake up early in the morning, and that motivation comes from the fact that you believe waking up early is going to produce a better state of affairs in your life than if you wake up late. So, you are trading the possibility to wake up late for waking up early, even though it's uncomfortable. In other words, you voluntarily create a moderate discomfort in the present for the sake of a better state of comfort in the future. Every single decision you make in your life is a trade. We trade by acting and by exchanging goods, services, and financial assets with other human beings. [04:04] Since we have to trade with the environment and other human beings if we want to achieve a better state of affairs, we will always attempt to make trades that enable us to have some sort of advantage, otherwise there is no reason to engage in such an exercise. However, when two human beings engage in a transaction, the transaction is only completed when both sides feel they are having some sort of advantage. That's the key to understand why markets are not a zero-sum game. [04:32] If you think about this situation mathematically, you will come to the conclusion that it's not possible for both ends of a transaction to have mutual advantage. The great thing about praxeology is that it adds the human factor to the understanding of economic systems, and by doing that, this mathematical paradox of mutual advantage simply vanishes away. If you think about a trade only in mathematical terms, you would think that for one side to have an advantage, the other must have a disadvantage. However, that's not how human beings and markets work. [05:06] To clarify this, we need two ideas: the delta between objective and subjective perception in a person, and the cognitive parallax between people. We have basically two layers through which we see the world: the objective and the subjective layer. And it's the combination of these two layers that motivate you to act. For example, you cannot engage in transactions if you only had the objective layer, because it's precisely the gap between objectivity and subjectivity that drives you towards action. [05:39] Let's look at a simple example. Imagine that person A has $20,000 and she wants to buy a car that costs exactly $20,000. There is no question about the price of the car, but the subjective interpretation of the car's value is going to determine if person A will buy the car or not. If the person subjectively perceives that the car is worth more than the $20,000 she has, she will engage in the transaction thinking that she's trading her $20,000 for something that is worth more than that. Another way of thinking about this is that the person believes that the car is more valuable than the $20,000 she has in her pocket. [06:20] On the other end of this possible transaction, there is person B, who wants to sell her car. Person B subjectively perceives that the car is worth less than $20,000. So, person A and person B will engage in a transaction, and both people will think they are getting out of the transaction with an advantage. Both people feel they moved toward a better state of affairs after the trade. If this situation was purely mathematical, this idea of mutual advantage would be a paradox. But as it turns out, the human factor makes it possible for mutual advantage to take place, which is the final nail in the coffin regarding the argument of whether or not markets are a zero-sum game. They are obviously not a zero-sum game. Both person A and person B have a gap in their objective/subjective layers of perception, and it's precisely this gap that drives them to engage in a trade. That's the delta or gap between the objective and subjective layers within a person. [07:23] However, notice that this gap manifests itself differently in different people. Person A thought the car was worth more than $20,000, and person B thought it was worth less than $20,000. This leads us to the idea of cognitive parallax between people. Human beings are complicated machines that vary quite dramatically in culture, cognitive ability, the specific calibration of heuristics, personality, status, preferences, the way they were raised, financial power, and so on. That means that two different people can perceive the exact same object or idea in completely different ways. This difference between how people perceive the same thing is called cognitive parallax. And we can observe that in the car example. There is a clear difference in how person A and person B perceive the same object. So, let's summarize what we have up to this point. [08:20] The Action Axiom leads to trade, but trades can only occur because of the delta between objective and subjective perception in the individual level, and the cognitive parallax between people. These two ideas also give rise to the concept of supply and demand because even though people vary a lot in their characteristics, we have groups of people who have more or less the same views and intuitions about ideas and objects. For example, there is a group of people in society that consumes pop music, and there is a group of people who consumes classical music. What leads these people to consume these specific products is that list of ways in which people differ. But the point is that there are groups of people with similar interpretations. People who want to buy something represent the demand because they are demanding something they value more than the money they already have. People who want to sell something represent supply because they are offering something they have in exchange for something else they value more. We can observe this effect in any market you can imagine and at any given price. In other words, in any price level of any market, we have people who think it's a good idea to sell and people who think it's a good idea to buy. Again, this is cognitive parallax. If everybody agreed about the value of a market, there would be no market at all because prices would not fluctuate. [09:45] Okay, so why does price move all the time? What causes price to move like it does in the price chart? The answer is the imbalance between supply and demand. When supply and demand are equal, prices don't change. Let me demonstrate that to you with a simple example. [10:01] Let's say that there are 1,000 people living in a small village, and each one of these people consumes 10 apples per month. We have 1,000 people demanding 10 apples per month each, so the total demand for apples in the village is 10,000 apples per month. We also have 10 apple producers in the village, and each one of them is able to produce 1,000 apples per month. That represents a total supply of 10,000 apples per month. Notice that the supply and demand are perfectly equal. And when that happens, everybody is satisfied and nobody feels that there is an opportunity to make money because there is no gap to fill. [10:40] Now, let's imagine that two of these apple producers move to another city for whatever reason, and the remaining producers cannot increase their capacity. We would have a demand for 10,000 apples and a supply of 8,000 apples. In other words, there would be an imbalance. In that case, two things can happen. Either new apple producers emerge to fill that gap, or the current apple producers increase the price to make the demand match the supply. Let's say that until now, each apple costs $1. At that price, the amount of people willing to buy apples was 1,000. However, if producers increase the price to $1.50, for example, there will be less people willing to buy apples, and the demand will decrease. [11:27] The essential point here is that whenever there is an imbalance between supply and demand, there is the opportunity to make money. Implying this idea is the fact that markets are always after the equilibrium. As fast as an imbalance appears, people will immediately try to make money from it. Another way of thinking about this is that whenever there is a difference or imbalance between supply and demand, people will realize that there is the opportunity to solve that imbalance by either opening new businesses or by changing the prices of the current market. [12:02] But how exactly does that work? How do prices actually change? The answer is something called the market auction. For price to move from one level to another, there is a specific and fair process that needs to take place. Let's assume a simple scenario once again to see how the market auction works. Imagine that we have the stock of company X. The price is currently $10 per share, and there is an imbalance between supply and demand. At $10, there is a demand for 1,000 shares and a supply of only 700 shares. The overlap in supply and demand will be exhausted, which means that out of the 1,000 shares that are being demanded, 700 of them will be traded since we have a 700-share supply at this price level. However, there is still a demand of 300 shares remaining, and there is no supply left at $10. So, now what? At $10, there is no supply left. But at $10.01, there is a supply of 450 shares, which means that no one wants to sell shares at $10 anymore, but some people would sell shares at a slightly higher price. In this case, the buyers who wanted to purchase shares at $10 have two choices: they can either accept the new price or not. If they don't accept a new price of $10.01, the demand will be lower at $10.01. However, if they accept the new price, the supply would be exhausted at $10.01. [13:34] Conclusion: What makes price move is when a player has to accept a new price offered by the other player due to the lack of liquidity in a specific price level. When the imbalance between supply and demand is too great, price will move a lot. For example, if there is too much demand and very sparse supply, the demand will eat the supply on its way up. The opposite is also true, of course. [14:00] This leads to the idea of highs and lows in a price chart, which are nothing more than places where the supply and demand balance was extremely tilted to one of the sides, and therefore, price had no alternative but to reverse direction. A low is a place where there was too much demand and very sparse supply. A high is a place where there was too much supply and very sparse demand. The distance between a low and a high is called price vector. Notice that price vectors sum the move of the price from point A to point B. However, unlike what most traders think, there are more points in the price vector beyond the extremes, and this is absolutely critical for trading. These logical deductions from the action axiom explain why prices fluctuate and how they fluctuate. It's important to remember also that despite their artificial connotation, markets are a natural reflection of how human beings behave. In that sense, trades, and therefore markets, are not an arbitrary human invention. They are a discovery of the best way human beings have to move towards a better state of affairs in a just way.

semanticAnalysis.mainConcept: The core concept is that financial markets are not arbitrary constructs but are a natural and logical consequence of fundamental human behavior, a principle explained by the Austrian economic theory of Praxeology. The video breaks this down by starting with the 'Action Axiom'—that humans purposefully act to improve their state of affairs. This leads to the necessity of 'trade' in every decision, where potential actions are weighed and one is chosen over others. This inherent nature of trading, combined with differing subjective valuations ('cognitive parallax'), creates the conditions for markets, where supply and demand are born from these diverse perceptions of value. Price movement is therefore not random but a direct result of the market auction process resolving imbalances between supply and demand.
semanticAnalysis.deeperMeaning: For a trader, this framework implies that the market is not a random, purely mathematical system but a deeply human one. Price charts are a visual representation of collective human action and decision-making under uncertainty. Understanding this means a trader should focus on identifying areas of extreme supply/demand imbalance (highs and lows), as these are the points where the 'auction' is forced to find a new price. The 'price vector' between these points represents a completed auction cycle. This perspective shifts the analytical focus from merely predicting numbers to understanding the underlying human behavior that creates those numbers. It suggests that markets are discoverable systems of logic rather than chaotic environments, and that profitable trading comes from identifying and exploiting the predictable patterns that emerge from these fundamental imbalances.
semanticAnalysis.educationalGoal: The video's objective is to establish a foundational, first-principles understanding of why markets exist and how prices move. Titled 'Level Zero', it serves as the philosophical and theoretical bedrock for a broader trading curriculum. By grounding market dynamics in Praxeology and the Action Axiom, it aims to demystify price action and present it as a logical, cause-and-effect process. This initial lesson is designed to equip the student with a core mental model of the market as an auction driven by human valuation, which will later be used to interpret more complex chart patterns, indicators, and trading strategies. It answers the fundamental 'why' of the market before subsequent lessons address the 'how' of trading it.
